Updated opinion six years later:
I still don't care about Faulkner, but I can see it being fully in character for the Foundation to include all this literary investigation as part of their due diligence research.
So now a neutral-vote.

Also, I think there is a plothole in the first section of Faulkner's story. The stable boy is mixed race, and general opinion is that the plantation owner (presumed white) is his father. Big twist is that the head house slave (presumed black) is his real daddy. So mom must have been white to make mixed offspring.

Thing is, it's a lot easier to objectively tell who the mother of a child is than the father. So the gossip-mongers should at least have known about white mommy. So why did the gossips think the father could have even possibly been white too?

There are plot devices that could explain this: plantation owner's daughter secretly gave her embarrassing baby to a slave woman to raise as her own, for one. But anything like that should have been included in the plot synopsis.

item.content:encoded:
As it stands, it's just barely above standard for Anomalous Item cataloging IMO

I've seen this point several times in the thread now. And while I take absolutely no issue with your vote (or anyone else's) on this article, this particular observation is sticking in my craw a little bit.

Foreword to the Log of Anomalous Items:

The SCP Foundation has discovered a substantial number of items which are simply too useless to merit further attention. This document may be used as a resource, should knowledge of these items become useful or necessary in the future.

In my mind, there's two criteria for something being in the Log rather than getting a mainlist number: The in-universe one, which is that the object is "useless" and nothing more can be learned from it other than it's weird, and the site one, which is "is this interesting enough to merit its own article".

I'm not going to get into whether this is "interesting" enough; that's for the community to decide (also, I'm, you know, biased). But as to the in-universe standard, I disagree completely. This is a skip created through unknown means by a major figure in the world literary scene, that has informed us of aspects of his life that the world was unaware of before now, and is continually transmitting new information. In my mind, this would absolutely merit research as an SCP item.

I don't want to single you out Vincent, because other people have made the same observation you have. But there's a sense that people have that there's this bright and clear "line" between Log item and Mainlist item. I disagree that it's that simple, and I certainly disagree that my article is somehow "barely over" this loosely defined threshold.

Anyway, I have absolutely no problem with your vote or anyone else's vote on this or any of my articles, and that goes for the criticism in the thread as well. But I take issue that there's this clear "anomalous enough" standard out there by which we judge things appropriate for the mainlist or not. I think it's an issue that may deserve its own separate discussion.

item.content:encoded:
Hehe, my area was medieval and Anglo Saxon verse; I have a love-hate relationship with American Lit in general (love= Turn of the Screw; hate= Daisy Miller) and Faulkner in particular.

That said, having any strong feelings about Faulkner or literature at all only added to the intrigue of this entry. This sorta redefines paranormal in the context of storytelling, and that is just damn cool. I'm really not seeing the disjunction/incompleteness some that comments are mentioning— this follows a few interesting, consistent themes throughout, WITHOUT hitting you over the head with an "ART=INSANITY" moral.

EDIT: I mean, just this—

Pages 679-798 represent the current "narrative" being transmitted by SCP-986, and consist of an exegesis of the Book of Thomas the Contender, a non-canonical document related to the biblical New Testament.

"The writer of this passage can't seem to make up his mind as to whether the lower self or the higher self is speaking. It's possibly related to an inexpert translation, a common problem among the early Gnostic scholars. What's to be done?"

I get as irritated by bullshit/slapped-together references to theology as other users do by bad science. I think this is the only scip I've read that uses the word "exegesis" or "early Gnostic scholars" 1) correctly and 2) as a part of a creepy paranormal coded text attributed to Faulkner.

item.content:encoded:
I'm personally shocked that any Lit Major could have any feelings about Faulkner that aren't positive! But I totally agree with you, besides that. This SCP just gives me a Lit Crit boner, and I cannot currently think of another that gave me one like this.

I love everything about this skip. Kalinin, it really feels like you have a good grasp of Faulkner's work, and that really strengthens this piece. I mean, jesus, there's miscegenation, weird ghostly females, and clear gothic themes. I know that doesn't really make or break the skip, but to someone who's familiar with Faulkner, that's just icing on the cake. The only thing to make this more Faulknerian would be if the burial rites conducted by the Native American woman weren't even correct for her tribe. (Speaking of this, if you could stomach trying to write like Faulkner, I think some sections of this would make a fucking stellar tale.)

As to the question of whether or not this is anomalous enough, I really would argue it is. I do agree with Cellar Door, however, that this is risky as hell. No one is dying in this skip. There's no monster, no radiation, no quantum mechanics, but I think it's all the stronger for it.

Well, this one is right up my alley. I prefer Lynchian weirdness to straightforward sinister any day, and I was a Lit major. I have a lot of not entirely positive feelings about Faulkner, but the careful details you've written into this are pretty nifty. This is a very multi-layered SCP, tone-wise, and I personally found the mood set by the "non-anomalous" story was a clever set-up for the coded section.

In short: I think this was a risky SCP to write and won't be universally appealing, but I am impressed by the careful crafting and it hits all my literary kinks. This is more surrealism than horror, but I think that has its place on the mainlist. We get technological/sciency SCPs pretty often— it's cool to see one that requires "personnel with an educational background in literary criticism and/or cryptography", it's a reminder of the breadth of content the Foundation has to be prepared to deal with.
